cite: Village of Port Jervis v. Close, 24 N.Y. St. Rep. 730
court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
notes: Municipal ordinance case sustaining a license requirement for auction sales; no bearing on letting rooms/dwellings for lodging or on boarding-house regulation.

cite: Brentman v. Note, 24 N.Y. St. Rep. 281
notes: Slander/interference-with-contract case; the fact that plaintiff 'let furnished rooms' is mentioned only as incidental background to a house sale and is never legally characterized by the court.

cite: Schork v. Moritz, 24 N.Y. St. Rep. 898
notes: Dispute over accord-and-satisfaction/receipt in termination of a commercial store lease; no lodging or boarding element.

cite: Avery v. New York Central & Hudson River Railroad, 26 N.Y. St. Rep. 279
notes: Covenant-running-with-the-land/easement dispute involving a hotel's access to an alley; concerns a lessee's standing to sue for obstruction, not the character of letting rooms.

cite: People ex rel. Annan v. Walsh, 26 N.Y. St. Rep. 554
notes: Peckham's dissent on rate-regulation of grain elevators/warehouses under Munn v. Illinois; discusses innkeepers only as an illustrative common-law category, not a lodging dispute.

cite: Ahern v. Steele, 26 N.Y. St. Rep. 295
notes: Nuisance-liability case about a defective pier passed by devise subject to a lease; the quoted 'lets the premises with a nuisance' language is general landlord-liability doctrine, not about lodging/boarding houses.
Criminal statutory-construction case on grand larceny from the person; 'sojourners' refers to travelers as crime victims, unconnected to letting rooms or boarding houses.
Married woman's separate-property rights in a grocery business run with her husband; no lodging or boarding element.

cite: Hine v. New York Elevated R. R. Co., 27 N.Y. St. Rep. 303
court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
notes: Abutting landowner's easement of light, air and access against an elevated railway; not about letting or occupying rooms/dwellings.

cite: Franklin v. Brown, 27 N.Y. St. Rep. 955
holding_summary: The Court of Appeals held that a one-year lease of a furnished dwelling house carries no implied covenant that the premises are fit for habitation, so a tenant could not withhold rent because noxious odors migrated in from a neighboring livery stable that neither the landlord nor the tenant knew of and that the landlord did not cause.

quotes.text: It involves a lease for the ordinary period of one year, instead of a few weeks or months -during the fashionable season.

We do not think that there was any covenant in the lease in question, implied either by common law or from the acts or relations of the parties, that extended to the grievance of which the- defendant complains.
It is uniformly held in this state that the lessee of real property must run the risk of its condition, unless he has an express agreement on the part of the lessor covering that subject.

notes: Occupancy was a full year, not a short letting, so duration_of_occupancy is left unclear rather than forced into nights/weeks/months; the court expressly distinguishes this ordinary annual furnished-house lease from the English short-term/watering-place furnished lettings (Smith v. Marrable) and treats it under ordinary lease rules, an incident-of-ownership result favorable to letting generally. who_was_letting left unclear because the record does not show whether Franklin occupied elsewhere or was a commercial lessor.

cite: O'Donnell v. McIntyre, 28 N.Y. St. Rep. 619
notes: Assault/battery arising from a dispute over possession of a house after a tax-title sale; attornment doctrine, not lodging or boarding.

cite: Murphy v. Commissioners of Emigration, 28 N.Y. 134
notes: Baggage-loss/respondeat-superior case against public emigration commissioners; the statute's licensing of runners 'for boarding houses and transportation lines' is recited only as background and is never adjudicated on its merits.
Waste/timber-cutting dispute between remaindermen and a life-tenant's contract vendee; unconnected to lodging or letting of dwellings.

cite: Lyon v. Davis, 32 N.Y. St. Rep. 340
court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
holding_summary: The General Term affirmed that a wife's claimed debt against her husband's estate was valid and properly preferred in his general assignment, where the debt arose from money she had earned in her own separate business of keeping boarders under an agreement that she would keep the profits while her husband paid for his own board.

quotes.text: I find that the $1,500 secured to the wife of the assignor was a, good and valid debt; that she earned the money in her separate business; that she kept boarders, under an agreement with her husband that she should have the profits of the business and that he would pay the rent for his board.
that she kept boarders, under an agreement with her husband that she should have the profits of the business and that he would pay the rent for his board.
We concur with the trial judge respecting the indebtedness of ]he assignor to his wife, and in his conclusion that the debt was croperly preferred in the assignment.

notes: Court enforces the wife's property right in profits earned by keeping boarders in the household, treating the practice as a legitimate separate business generating a valid, preferable debt -- supports the favorable line that householder lodging/boarding arrangements are given legal effect. Duration of the boarding arrangement itself is not stated in the facts.

cite: Wittenbrock v. Mabius, 32 N.Y. St. Rep. 819
court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
notes: Deposition-subpoena case construing 'sojourner' for purposes of witness residency under the Code; concerns a commuting businessman, not a lodger or boarding-house occupant.

holding_summary: The Court of Appeals held that an innkeeper is an insurer of a guest's property committed to his custody and is liable for its loss by fire of unknown origin, unless the loss is attributable to the guest's own negligence or fraud, or to the act of God or the public enemy.

quotes.text: An innkeeper is an insurer of property, committed to his custody by a guest, unless the loss be due to the culpable negligence or fraud of the guest, or to the act of God or the public enemy.

We are of opinion that the judgment should be affirmed, on the ground that the testator was an insurer of the property committed to his charge, and that its loss has not been traced to either of the causes recognized as creating an exception to the general rule of liability.
The considerations of public policy in which the rule had its origin, forbid any relaxation of its rigor.

notes: A traveler (Banks, hauling goods overnight) lodged at the Balding House inn and lost property in a fire. The case is squarely about commercial innkeeping's distinct strict-insurer liability rather than the favorable/adverse axes of householder letting or police-power licensing of boarding houses, so polarity is marked mixed rather than favorable or adverse.

cite: City of Utica v. Churchill, 33 N.Y. 161
notes: National bank stockholder taxation case; discussion of ownership/incidents-of-ownership concerns bank shares and government bonds, not real property or lodging.

cite: Thorn v. Sutherland, 33 N.Y. St. Rep. 408
notes: Conversion action over trade fixtures left on a coal-yard lot after a commercial lease's surrender; no lodging or boarding element.
